headline: High: shared filesystem and MCP/tool-use create prompt-injection, leakage, and write-conflict pathways; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent B reads/writes workspace files and uses MCP with user-approved tool calls. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge via shared files or MCP outputs. The pathway is not proven by sandbox evidence, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF agent A writes attacker-controlled text into a workspace file that agent B later parses as instructions, injection is possible.
IF both agents are connected to the same MCP server without provenance tracking, prompt injection risk increases.
mitigations: Disable shared MCP servers for the pair.
Route A and B through separate workspaces.
Require explicit human review before B executes file-derived instructions.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages.
requires-engineering: enforce instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B explicitly reads and writes workspace files, and agent A touches code, repository metadata, and task prompts while also using MCP/GitHub. If they share a workspace, A’s outputs can expose sensitive context to B’s model backend or vice versa. The profiles do not show PHI, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF A and B share the same filesystem workspace, files from one can be read by the other.
IF either agent uploads file contents to a remote model provider, workspace data can leave the host.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Restrict B to a read-only clone when possible.
Keep secrets out of shared project files.
Use local-only models for sensitive tasks.
requires-engineering: add per-agent filesystem ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses; A can also modify git state, while B can write the filesystem and shares state via filesystem across instances. That is a direct overlapping-write pathway with no locking mechanism shown, so concurrent edits and git corruption are plausible in default use.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository directory, concurrent writes can race.
IF A modifies git state while B writes workspace files, repository corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Run only one writer at a time.
Assign separate branches per agent.
Use file locks around shared outputs.
Pause B while A performs git operations.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate analysis through MCP and shell workflows, and B is a chat/autocomplete IDE assistant that can act on workspace context. If B treats A’s outputs as authoritative, errors can cascade into code changes or operational actions. The profiles show a plausible handoff but not a fully automated action chain, so medium fits.
conditions: IF B consumes A’s generated text as ground truth without verification, downstream mistakes can propagate.
IF A’s outputs are copied into B’s editor context, B may optimize around incorrect assumptions.
mitigations: Require B to cite source files before acting.
Add a verification step before edits are applied.
Keep A’s outputs in a separate review buffer.
Use diff-based review for all generated changes.
requires-engineering: implement confidence-gated action policies.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and the profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch. A handles Ed25519 signatures and B handles model-provider API keys, but no regulated data class like PHI or EU PII is documented. The only concrete compliance concern is general logging/retention ambiguity, which is low.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into shared workspace files, compliance review becomes necessary.
IF either agent is configured with a noncompliant remote model provider, policy obligations may change.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Document retention settings for both tools.
Use approved model providers only.
Review logs for secret exposure.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and retention.
